concepts.name: Capital Account vs. Current Account: Definitional Boundary
key_dimensions: What constitutes a capital account transaction vs. current account transaction under FEMA 1999
Why transfer of ownership of assets/liabilities is the distinguishing criterion
UPSC trap: Remittances and transfers that appear capital but are classified as current (e.g., personal remittances)
Residual principle: anything not in current account defaults to capital account under FEMA

concepts.name: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): Definition, Routes, and Thresholds
key_dimensions: 10% ownership threshold distinguishing FDI from FPI — significance and international convention
Automatic route vs. Government route: sector-specific applicability and approval authority (DPIIT)
FDI in LLP, partly paid shares, warrants — newer instruments and their regulatory treatment
UPSC trap: FDI allowed sectors with caps (e.g., insurance 74%, defence 74%, multi-brand retail 51%) vs. prohibited sectors

concepts.name: Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI): Structure and Regulatory Framework
key_dimensions: SEBI's FPI Regulations 2019: three-category classification (Category I, II — abolition of Category III)
Instruments accessible to FPIs: equities, corporate bonds, G-secs, T-bills, municipal bonds
Aggregate FPI limit in G-secs and corporate bonds — Medium Term Framework (MTF)
UPSC trap: FPI vs. FII vs. QFI — historical evolution and current unified FPI regime

concepts.name: External Commercial Borrowings (ECB): Framework and Tracks
key_dimensions: Three tracks: ECB Track I (medium-term foreign currency), Track II (long-term foreign currency), Track III (INR-denominated) — and their end-use stipulations
Eligible borrowers and recognized lenders under RBI's ECB framework
All-in-cost ceiling: benchmark (SOFR/LIBOR successor) + spread cap by maturity
UPSC trap: end-use restrictions — ECB cannot be used for real estate, equity investment in India, on-lending except for specific NBFCs; Masala bonds as a subset of Track III

concepts.name: Masala Bonds: Nature, Issuance, and Risk Characteristics
key_dimensions: Definition: INR-denominated bonds issued overseas — currency risk borne by foreign investor, not Indian issuer
Regulatory oversight: RBI guidelines + SEBI listing requirements for overseas exchanges (LSE, SGX)
Difference from vanilla ECB: no hedging cost for issuer; investor bears exchange rate risk
UPSC trap: Masala bonds classified under ECB (capital account) NOT under portfolio investment; first issuer (IFC, 2014) vs. first corporate issuer (HDFC)

concepts.name: Non-Resident Indian (NRI) Deposits: NRE, NRO, and FCNR(B) Accounts
key_dimensions: NRE (Non-Resident External): INR account, fully repatriable principal + interest, interest tax-free in India
NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary): INR account, restricted repatriability (USD 1 million/year), interest taxable
FCNR(B) (Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank): foreign currency term deposit, fully repatriable, no exchange risk for depositor
UPSC trap: NRE and FCNR(B) are capital account transactions; NRO receipts from Indian sources are current account — critical classification trap

concepts.name: Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS): Scope, Limits, and Restrictions
key_dimensions: Current limit: USD 250,000 per financial year per resident individual for permissible current and capital account transactions
Capital account uses permitted: overseas direct investment, purchase of property abroad, opening foreign bank accounts
TCS (Tax Collected at Source) applicability on LRS remittances above threshold — Finance Act 2023 changes
UPSC trap: LRS available only to resident individuals NOT corporates/firms/trusts; remittance for prohibited purposes (margin trading, lottery) not allowed

concepts.name: Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) by Indian Entities
key_dimensions: Definition: Indian resident investing in foreign entity through equity, loan, or guarantee
Financial commitment limit: 400% of net worth of Indian party under automatic route
Distinction between ODI (strategic/ownership stake ≥10%) vs. Overseas Portfolio Investment (OPI) — new FEMA ODI Rules 2022
UPSC trap: Round-tripping concern — ODI to jurisdictions with secrecy laws; GIFT City entities and their ODI treatment

concepts.name: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 1999: Capital Account Convertibility Architecture
key_dimensions: FEMA vs. FERA: shift from criminal to civil offence; from control to management of foreign exchange
Section 6 of FEMA: capital account transactions — RBI power to specify permissible transactions and limits
Full Capital Account Convertibility (FCAC): Tarapore Committee I (1997) and II (2006) — preconditions not yet met
UPSC trap: India has CURRENT account convertibility (Article VIII of IMF) but NOT full capital account convertibility; partial/calibrated convertibility is the current status

concepts.name: American Depository Receipts (ADR) and Global Depository Receipts (GDR): Capital Flow Mechanism
key_dimensions: Mechanism: Indian company issues shares to overseas depository bank which issues ADR/GDR to foreign investors
ADR listed on US exchanges (NYSE/NASDAQ); GDR listed on European exchanges (Luxembourg, London)
Classified as FDI in Indian BoP statistics when underlying shares represent fresh capital raising
UPSC trap: Two-way fungibility of ADR/GDR — conversion back to underlying shares allowed subject to RBI/SEBI guidelines; tax treatment under India-US DTAA for ADR holders

concepts.name: Special Drawing Rights (SDR): Reserve Asset and Allocation Mechanism
key_dimensions: SDR as international reserve asset created by IMF — not a currency, but a claim on freely usable currencies
SDR basket composition: USD, EUR, CNY, JPY, GBP — weights revised every 5 years
SDR allocations appear on BOTH sides of capital account: as reserve asset (asset) and as SDR allocation (liability)
UPSC trap: 2021 COVID-19 special SDR allocation of USD 650 billion — India's share (~$17.86 billion) credited to RBI; SDR interest rate = weighted average of short-term rates of basket currencies

concepts.name: Foreign Exchange Reserves: Composition and Management by RBI
key_dimensions: Four components: Foreign currency assets (FCA), Gold, SDRs, Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) in IMF
RTP: India's quota contribution to IMF in foreign currency — can be drawn unconditionally, hence a reserve asset
RBI's reserve management: safety > liquidity > returns (SLR framework) — investment in sovereign bonds of reserve currencies
UPSC trap: FCA expressed in USD but held in multiple currencies (EUR, GBP, JPY etc.) — valuation changes affect FCA even without transactions; gold held partly abroad (Bank of England)

concepts.name: Balance of Payments (BoP): Capital and Financial Account Structure under IMF BPM6
key_dimensions: IMF BPM6 (6th edition): Financial Account replaces 'Capital Account' for investment flows; old 'Capital Account' becomes narrow (capital transfers + acquisition/disposal of non-produced assets)
Financial account sub-components: FDI, FPI, Other Investment (loans, trade credit, NRI deposits), Financial Derivatives, Reserve Assets
UPSC trap: India's BoP presentation by RBI still uses 'Capital Account' terminology colloquially for both capital + financial account — misalignment with BPM6 terminology
Sign convention trap: Surplus in capital/financial account = net capital inflows (capital account credit) — opposite logic to current account

concepts.name: Participatory Notes (P-Notes): Mechanism, Regulation, and Controversy
key_dimensions: P-Notes (Offshore Derivative Instruments): FPIs issue these to overseas investors not registered with SEBI, with underlying Indian securities
Regulatory journey: SEBI's crackdown post-2007 (Sebi circular requiring KYC of P-Note holders); 2017 restrictions tightening
Concern: anonymity of end-beneficiary enabling round-tripping and money laundering through P-Notes
UPSC trap: P-Notes are NOT banned — still legal but heavily regulated; P-Note holders cannot vote or have ownership rights in underlying Indian companies

concepts.name: Voluntary Retention Route (VRR) for FPI Investment in Debt
key_dimensions: VRR introduced by RBI in 2019: FPIs commit to retain minimum 75% of allocated amount for minimum 3 years in Indian debt
Incentive: FPIs under VRR exempted from macro-prudential limits and concentration limits applicable to regular FPI debt route
Separate from General Investment Limit (GIL) — additionality to deepen Indian debt market
UPSC trap: VRR available for both G-secs and corporate bonds; retention period and minimum retention percentage — distinguish from regular FPI debt limits

concepts.name: Fully Accessible Route (FAR) for G-sec Investment
key_dimensions: FAR (2020): Specified Government securities open to non-residents without any limit — part of India's G-sec index inclusion strategy
Motivation: inclusion in global bond indices (JP Morgan GBI-EM from June 2024, Bloomberg EM Index)
Difference from regular FPI G-sec route: no quantitative limit under FAR; specific securities designated by RBI
UPSC trap: FAR does NOT replace FPI route for G-secs — both routes coexist; FAR is specifically for index-eligible bonds; capital flow implications of index inclusion for INR and BoP

concepts.name: Trade Credit: Short-term and Long-term as Capital Account Component
key_dimensions: Trade credit = credit extended by overseas supplier/buyer for import/export transactions
Short-term trade credit (up to 1 year for non-capital goods, 3 years for capital goods) regulated by RBI under ECB framework
Classified under 'Other Investment' in financial account of BoP — often overlooked as capital flow

UPSC trap: Trade credit is NOT the same as export credit given by Indian banks to exporters (which is current account related financing); RBI's all-in-cost ceiling applies to trade credit just like ECB

concepts.name: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs): FPI Access
key_dimensions: SEBI allowed FPIs to invest in units of REITs and InvITs — classified as FPI flows in capital account
REITs: must distribute 90% of net distributable cash flow — yield instrument attracting foreign capital
InvITs: infrastructure assets monetization vehicle — government used to attract foreign pension/sovereign funds
UPSC trap: Foreign investment in REITs/InvITs classified as FPI (not FDI) even if strategic stake — threshold-based classification; GIFT City-domiciled InvITs have different regulatory treatment

concepts.name: Capital Controls: Instruments, Rationale, and India's Calibrated Approach
key_dimensions: Types: price-based (Tobin tax, withholding tax) vs. quantity-based (FPI sectoral limits, ECB end-use restrictions)
Rationale for capital controls: prevent sudden stop/reversal, manage exchange rate volatility, prevent asset price bubbles (Trilemma — impossible trinity)
India's approach: asymmetric controls — inflows more liberalized than outflows (ODI restrictions tighter than FDI inflow rules)

UPSC trap: IMF's evolving position — from opposing capital controls (Washington Consensus) to 'Integrated Policy Framework' (2022) accepting controls as legitimate tool; India's position in IMF debates

concepts.name: Suriname Bonds / Rupee-denominated Sovereign Bonds and Bilateral Currency Arrangements
key_dimensions: India's push for INR internationalization: INR invoicing of trade, Vostro accounts for INR trade settlement (RBI July 2022 framework)
Vostro accounts: foreign banks holding INR accounts in Indian banks — surplus INR can be invested in G-secs and T-bills (capital account implication)
Distinction: Rupee trade settlement (current account) vs. foreign investment of surplus Vostro balances in Indian securities (capital account)
UPSC trap: Vostro account investment in G-secs does NOT bypass FPI limits currently — RBI has set separate limits; this is distinct from Masala bonds and from FAR route
